## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Matarodanajātaka* (Ja 317) is a canonical birth story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddakanikāya [SuttaCentral]. According to the prose framework edited by V. Fausböll, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana concerning a landowner (*kuṭumbika*) living in Sāvatthī whose brother had died [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. Overcome with grief, the landowner ceased bathing and eating and went weeping to the cemetery every morning [Fausböll 1883]. The teaching opens with the verse phrase *Matamataṁ eva rodatha* ("Weep for the dead / Weep for the living") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to remove sorrow, and the Buddha similarly brought his hearer to peace; upon the exposition of the four truths at the conclusion of the teaching, the bereaved landowner established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1883]. In the identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the wise instructor of the past who dispelled the grief of the multitude (*nissokakarapaṇḍita*) as himself [Fausböll 1883].
SuttaCentral notes four modern translations across four languages and lists no cross-corpus parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus indicates no cross-language matches with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora, but documents four Pali-internal text-reuse matches with the commentary in the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (encompassing 840 characters, with the longest alignment spanning segments §0.4–4.4 to §434_12–446 with 0.92 similarity) [DharmaNexus].
